blocks.x: I've heard every pianist in the world, every one of them, and I never will forget that you used to say, well, I can get ideas from every pianist. He might sound very mediocre, but I'll find something that I can put in my ideas. I've never seen or heard anybody even hold a candle to you. Well, there's only two people that I know of that really thought that my playing was just, you know, on top of everybody and anything, and that was you. That's what's funny, Jack. That's right, that's right. But the thing is that I'm in my place for it. I want to get better and better. But I like you used to say, well, give me five more years, and I'll record or something like that. You know, Jack, when I was young, I thought I'd be in Playgood. That's gone for 38 years. Yeah, I see. When I was young, when I was young, I thought I was going to be in Playgood, you know? Oh, hell. But as I went along and went along, you know, I couldn't be, you know, I wasn't going to be in Playgood. I've heard every pianist in the world, every one of them. And I never will forget that you used to say, well, I can get ideas from every pianist. It might not be, it might sound very mediocre, but I'll find something that I can put in my ideas. And I've never seen or heard anybody even hold a candle to you. Well, there's only two people that I know of that really thought that my playing was just, you know, on top of everybody and anything. And that was you and I was playing. Oh, that isn't true. I can say anything you know of the people offhand, like the Kremas, everybody we ever talked to who has ever heard you play, people that you may respect their talent, or maybe you don't, but like Bob McCracken, I mean, who honestly believe in you and your talent. Well, say, incidentally, Bob McCracken was fired here about last year. I know he was, yeah. You know, I want to get a match. Yeah, right. Here's him. You got some match I want to say? Mm-hmm. But, uh, old Blanton, I couldn't, I couldn't do anything wrong. Well, to me, he is. I can't do anything wrong with Jack. That's right. You know what I mean? Well, I feel that way about my playing at times. Now, you know what I mean? Lots of trombones admire my work that are wonderful trombones, you know? And I say, well, gee whiz, I'm nervous. Maybe he's just curious about it. But, uh, I get the same. You know, Jack, it's once you get out of anything that counts, you know what I mean? Yeah. It's not whether anything is good or bad. That's, those are just the way. Well, no, not only that, but look, uh, look at, uh, uh, I'd like to see the world share your talent. You know what I mean? To hear you. Now, that's the truth. Jack, in that idea, the world is very small. It shrinks, you know? Mm-hmm. Jack, in that idea, the world is very small. And I'll just say, from an entertainment standpoint, you know? Yes. The people will get a, possibly a, a lot of kick and a lot of fun and that. Not believe in fun. Yes. Yes. You know what I mean? And also joy and joy and joy. You know what I mean? So clean and fun. But the thing about it is, uh, it's just which way each person wants to go, you know? Yeah. Now, uh, in myself, of course, I have a different set of... Okay.
It's an interview being recorded in the back room of the Dream Room in the 400 block of Bourbon Street. And what's the date, Jack? October?
Uh, this is, uh, the 29th of, uh, October, 1959.
And, uh, my name's Dick Allen, so you give yours, too.
Jack T. Yorden. And what's your name?
I'm Paul Crawford. Okay, fine. We got that. Now, where were you born, Jack?
Well, I was born over in Vernon, Texas, in 1905. That's a little town in the northern part of, northwestern part of Texas, near the Oklahoma border in Wilburga County.
Mm-hmm. And the exact date of your birth?
Uh, August the 20th, 1905. August the 20th. 1905. Yeah, I'm 54 years old.
Mm-hmm. And, uh, what kind of music do you remember hearing first over there?

Well, uh, my mother was a piano teacher, and, uh, the, one of the professors in town, uh, by the name of, uh, Paul Getze, late Paul Getze, uh, is a, he was a, a German-born, uh, professor, and very well schooled. And, uh, we had a little orchestra there, and we played light classics, of, uh, maybe, uh, type of humorous and, and, uh, barcarole and things like that. And then we had a, a little hometown brass band. It was always there to, uh, give a little, uh, outdoor concerts during the summer, and play for the county fair, and, uh, maybe sometime for a parade or something. And they needed a trombone in this, uh, little hometown band. So, when I was seven years old, they got me a trombone, and, uh, thought they could just raise one. So, I took up the trombone at the age of seven, and, uh, I've been playing trombone ever since.
Play any other instruments?

Well, I, I, I know the valve instruments. That's the trumpet and the baritone, and, uh, and, uh, the French horn and so forth. All, all the brass instruments I can play. And, uh, took a little piano from my mother, but, uh, I didn't care much for the piano. In those, uh, early years, uh, especially in Vernon, Texas, most pianists, uh, were the girls. And, uh, I don't know, I couldn't get it in my, in my, uh, head. It should be played by a boy. It seemed like a girl's instrument. And, I, I wanted to play the trombone.
Did they ever play any funerals with brass bands over there?

Not in Texas. I don't think that, uh, I don't know of any place in Texas where they ever did that. That's customary in, uh, New Orleans. Uh, here in Louisiana is about the only place I think they ever did in the United States. Uh, uh, this little band, uh, that we had didn't, uh, didn't do much for us, for me, rather, in the way of the jazz field. But, I was sort of, uh, I had ideas of my own. I could hear chords. I could hear harmony. And, I had a pretty good ear and a little talent. And, put them all together. Uh, I guess I might have annoyed the bandmaster a little bit by, uh, sort of, uh, filling in. And, uh, so, uh, kind of bluesing it up a little bit, everything, you know. However, he, uh, used to kind of admire me for doing it. He says, uh, it's not written that way, but it sounds alright. I think that I got my, uh, influence from the spirituals more than anything. If there was ever a revival meeting around, I used to try and get around, sneak around, and listen in to the music as much as I could. And, that seemed to be the thing that came natural to me.
Well, what churches would this be in? What kind? Well, Baptist Methodist or what?

Uh, the spirituals, uh, was, uh, always from the Negroes when they'd have camp meetings. And, uh, revival meetings. However, I used to play in the Christian church in Vernon, Texas. Every Sunday I'd have a little solo worked up. And, uh, but that was a little type, different type of music that was for the choir. Uh, I think that, uh, we'll continue after just a few minutes, huh?
Okay, whenever you're ready. Well, how did you learn trombone and develop your style? That's what I really like to know.

Well, I'll tell you, when I was, uh, pretty young, my mother and I used to play in, uh, the old silent movie theaters. We used to play for the comedies and, uh, I don't know, just trombone and piano. You know, learn more technique because I had the whole, swing the whole thing, melody and all. You know. And, uh, my mother played very good ragtime piano, which was very good for those years. Then, uh, I lost my father in 1918 with the flu. And then I went, we went to Oklahoma City. And I went one more year of, uh, school. And I went down to, uh, San Angelo to stay with my uncle. Because, uh, my mother was having a pretty rough time with us four kids, uh, making ends meet. So I went to San Angelo and worked in a theater as an operator and, uh, worked in his hillbilly band. And I went to San Angelo and, uh, I don't know, I was, I guess, uh, uh, sort of a repetition was, uh, by the word of mouth, I guess, got around. That there was, you had over in San Angelo and maybe had a little Tylenol trombone. So I got an offer to go to San Antonio. So in 1920, I went to San Antonio. And I worked in a place called Horn Palace with Terry Shan on piano and myself and banjo and drums. And, uh, I don't remember the other two. I worked there for a while and then there was a big flood. Uh, just almost, uh, wrecked San Antonio in 1921. So I went over and joined Peg Kelly in Houston. And, uh, and Peg, uh, was in those days about 40 years ahead on his piano playing. He just played wonderful. And, uh, everything I know I learned, I think, from Peg Kelly. So I stayed in Houston with him a while. And, uh, when things would get, uh, kind of, uh, quiet around Houston, sometimes I'd go up and work with Dr. Ross around Wichita Falls. And, uh, and I, he wanted to go to New York to see a friend of his, Willard Robinson. I knew him very well, too. And, uh, so we went to New York in 1927. And, uh, I've stayed up there ever since. I was very fortunate. And, uh, the very first thing meeting a dear old friend of mine, William and Norman. And, uh, he introduced me to Red Nickels and Miff Moll and, uh, Joe Van Ute and all of them. And then through, uh, them, they, we had a jam session and they liked my work. And, uh, and then on I did, you know, Red Nickels, uh, Five Penny records. And Miff Moll did the first ones. And then I came on and did the rest. And then I went with, uh, Benny Pollock. Which at that time had a wonderful band for a big band. It was, uh, uh, a band that could play big arrangements, fine arrangements, but turn around and, uh, play anything. There was a little kid with us, uh, the name of Benny Goodman. In those days he was about 18 years old. Jimmy McPartland and, uh, Bud Freeman. Ray Baduke, who's a New Orleans boy here, was, we got him on drums so Benny could, uh, uh, stand in front with a baton. And we went to the Park Central Hotel. We stayed there about a year. And, uh, and then when the 1929 crash, uh, the, the hotel discontinued music. And, uh, I stayed with Pollock until 1933. In the meantime, Benny Goodman had dropped out. Matty Metlock had taken his place. Bud Freeman had left. And, uh, Eddie Miller had taken his place. He was a band in the United States. And, uh, Hilton Lamar, I call it Nappy Lamar now. He was with us on the guitar. And, uh, that's the way it was up until about 1933 when I left. And I went with Paul Whiteman. Uh, so the, the band, uh, pulled away from Pollock. Uh, Pollock wanted to go to the West Coast and, uh, open a restaurant anyway. And they got Bob Crosby in the front of the band. And I stayed in Whiteman about, uh, from 33 to 39, six years. And I got a big band. I had, uh, 16 pieces. One time I had 18. And, uh, that was about the time that Harry James started and, uh, Gene Krupa. And, uh, so that, that was some of the finest years of swinging right along in there.

Can we back up for a minute and go back to your early period? Yeah. Because there's some particular people I'd like to ask you about some particular things. What kind of training did Peg Kelly have that he should develop this wonderful style?

Well, he's self-taught, but he used to listen to, uh, everybody that came through Houston. Especially, there used to be quite a few colored boys that come through Houston, you know, from New Orleans. Yeah. And there was quite, quite a lot of, uh, entertainment in that city at that time. And, uh, I guess he picked up a little bit here and there from everybody and they put it all with his own. And, uh, it was fantastic when I first heard him and, uh, I guess he still is now. I saw him just a few weeks ago. I didn't hear him play because, uh, his piano at home is, uh, not in very good condition. But, uh, they tell me that he keeps up his practice every day. On, sometimes on a silent keyboard and, and what time he goes out. But he doesn't work professionally anymore.

You know, he seems to me to have been so wonderful and to develop a lot of things that, you know, from what I've heard from Len Harrell and guys who listen to him. Yeah. Yeah. Like the guy who worked with Jimmy Joy, Len Harrell, I'm talking about. Yeah. He must have heard a lot of classical music too, huh?

Yeah. He went, he made a, he made a real study of piano. He used to practice about eight hours a day. And, uh, he taught himself to read and then he, uh, went for Chopin mostly. And, uh, of course, uh, Debussy and, uh, and Ravel. And he made, uh, put all this with his ideas. And, uh, of course he knows Boogie Woogie and, uh, and the Earl Hines style of piano. He was playing long before, way before Earl Hines. And I guess it, uh, never been heard by anybody. He was sort of, uh, Art Tatum maybe. Uh, Art Tatum and Earl Hines together. And that's Walter, near as I can describe it. And you put them with, their ideas with, uh, Debussy's, uh, themes and things. Well, it's, it's tremendous. And he used to leave me and just fell down. I mean, I could listen to him play for a while and it would, uh, I couldn't hardly get up out of a chair. It was, uh, like a real, uh, a real wonderful moving picture. It would, uh, for, you know, that makes you laugh and you cry. And there's so many emotions that goes with your listening to him play that it leaves you just worn out.

Well, to me, and when I listen to your style, I see that you have developed such a clean technique and developed the trombone so much further than the people that were before you. I believe myself. Yeah.

Well, I remember when I was a little kid, uh, hearing, uh, the trombone, I used to think they were just murdering the instrument by sliding around on the trombone. And, uh, initially they were, they were just hunting for the note, you know, and, uh, they would just clown it up when they couldn't find it. And, I always thought that if I couldn't play it clean and right, I wasn't going to play it at all. And, uh, of course I learned a lot of shortcuts because in, in my early years my arms weren't very long. And I had to make, uh, uh, different, uh, positions and things that, uh, in some notes, in the lower positions, I had to leave out entirely. And, uh, then one fortunate thing, uh, I started on a high pitch horn. It used to have two, uh, different, uh, standard pitches. There was one called standard and there was one called international or orchestra pitch. And they were half a tone apart. Well, I had the wrong horn. I had the high pitch horn. I was playing it with the piano. So, I learned to play in, uh, when the piano was in B flat, I'd be in A. And, uh, when the piano was in F, I'd be in E. And, I think that, uh, turned out to be a fortunate mistake instead of a holdback. Because, now I can look back at those keys that I used to have to play in, and it makes it come easier now. You played with, uh, string, you said, with the hillbilly band, too. They play in a lot of sharp keys. Yeah, yes, they do. And, uh, see, I was the only instrument up in that thinly populated area in Vernon and San Angelo. I'd be the only instrument, you know, besides piano and banjo and drums. So, uh, I could play the melody and, uh, and play a chorus, that lib. And when you play it in turkey and straw and things like that, it's really technical. You know, it's a, it's a kind of a hillbilly. I mean, it's not too easy. Well, it, uh, I think it was a good start. Rather, it'd be, it was kind of crude, but it was a good start for a person that had to be self-taught.
Well, how did you develop those lip, uh, all the different things you do with your lip in one position? I don't know what you call them, Paul. I'll have to ask you about those technical names.

Well, those, uh, thirds and sixths, I've, I've had a good lip, a good control, but, uh, I have a good ear. That's the main thing. I, I have to hear both. I have to hear the chord, and then I know what I want. I don't stop to think of what chord it is, but, uh, I, uh, automatically, um, my arm goes to the, the, any note in the chord. And, uh, in any chord, you'll find a thirds that you can make triplets on that, that is not too hard. It, uh, it's all, and being fast enough, and coordination enough, is when you change chords to get the right one. I mean, it might be, uh, from the tonic to the third in one place, and then maybe from the third to the fifth in another chord. It, uh, it's, uh, it, it's all ear. It's all what it is. And I've always had good pitch. They call it perfect pitch. Uh, I can hear any kind of a sound, from a motor or anything, and tell you what note it is, and I'm sure. I'll tell you what note it is, and, uh, that helps. Because I depend on my ear for everything. But I was fortunate. I learned to read first, because it's usually pretty hard to learn to read after you, after you once got started, uh, by ear entirely. So it all came along together, and, uh, accidentally, and through handicaps, it turned out to be better.
I was wondering about, uh, rap. When did you first meet Leon Rapolo?

When I was with Peck Kelly, we needed a clarinetist over in Houston, and, uh, we needed a trumpet player, too. We got Leon Rapolo, and we got Leon Prima first, who was the trumpet player. And then, uh, he recommended Leon Rapolo. And Leon Rapolo came over and worked with us over at Houston.
What years was this about?

About 1924. Which was one of the last jobs, I guess, Rapolo played before he lost his health. He was over there, and he was a wonderful clarinetist. Strictly a faker. He didn't read, I know. And, uh, but it was the beginning of, uh, jazz clarinet. Benny Goodman and all of them. Heard him when he went to Chicago with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. And, uh, of course, right away, they, uh, that gave them the idea of what a clarinet should sound like. And with their technique, but went with it, that's what made those kids so wonderful.
Now, uh, how did Leon Prima play in those years? Very good.

He played very good. What did he do? Go ahead. Well, I'll tell you. If you've heard, uh, William Manone, you'd probably— William Manone plays an authentic New Orleans style, and so did Leon Rapolo—I mean, Leon Prima in those days.

Would you call it, what they called goofus in those days, or would you call it, uh, like— We'd call it hot, hot trumpet. Hot trumpet, you'd call it. Yeah. Uh-huh. And that's what he was playing. Yeah. Um, did you ever know Charlie Cordella or Red Bowman or Sidney Ayrton?

Yes, I worked with all of them, too. Um, well, they were over in San Antonio. Worked in a little, uh, road spot, tavern, and, uh, there was Terry Shan and Charlie Cordella and Red Bowman and, uh, Sidney Ayrton, and they sent for me, and I went over to join them in San Antonio. And we worked together for, oh, a year or so, I guess. I've known Charlie ever since, Charlie Cordella, but I haven't seen him this trip. I understand he's still here in New Orleans.
That's right. So is Red, I believe.
Is he? Raymond Barton told me. He went, uh, down around Biloxi for a while. But I haven't seen, uh, either one, either Red Bowman or, uh, Charlie Cordella this trip.
How was Ayrton playing in those days?
Just like Rapolo. Just like Rapolo. They were almost identical. Very, very good.
Oh, back in your early days, what were the first records you remember that sounded like jazz to you?

Well, I think the very first record I remember was Louisiana Five. They had, uh, Al Nunez, who had clarinet. It was a five-piece band, just clarinet and rhythm. And I think he had trombone. I don't remember who it was. Then, uh, the original Dixeland Jazz Band was very fine. And, uh, then, uh, I remember Ted Lewis. I remember Ted Lewis, as you know, was probably a little different style. But, uh, he was one of the first jazz bands on record anyway.
That mighty fine trombone playing with it, too. Yes.

Mm-hmm. But we were playing, uh, I don't know, uh, we were playing just the same over with Peck. Of course, Peck was a better pianist, and, uh, so, uh, maybe we had an edge on, on the Dixeland band in that respect. But, uh, and I know that I played practically the same trombone as I do now. Uh, I think that things were going, uh, more or less in, uh, from the Texas side, just about as good as they were over here.
Well, you certainly had wonderful bands over there.

Yes, we did. Harry James is from Texas, and Ray McKinley is from Texas, and, uh, Jimmy Joy, of course. Jimmy Maloney played wonderful clarinet. He's from Texas. It turned out some very good boys over there. Oh, we sure did.
Alfonso Trent? Yeah. It's a good band everybody says. I never got a chance to hear it.
It was a good one.
And Boots and his buddies, too, over there in the thirties. I guess that was a good swing band. Uh-huh. Um, when did you first meet Wingy?

Well, I was with Doc Bross, and we were working out of Albuquerque, New Mexico. And he came through there, and, uh, you know, the trains used to stop for lunch in Albuquerque. And I was living in a hotel right across from the station, and he heard, he'd heard about me. So, during this 30-minute lunch period, he came over to the hotel and looked me up. And this was, uh, about 1923 or something like that. And he was on his way out to join a fellow in Phoenix by the name of Ham Crawford. So I said, well, if you get out there and you don't find everything to your liking, and you want to make a change, well, I can swing it with Doc Bross if he'd come back and join us. And he did. So we worked together quite a while. That was 1925 when he came back to work with us. That's the last when I worked with him. And I came to New Orleans. He sent for me to come down here to New Orleans and Biloxi, along about 1925. I actually left Doc Bross, and he came down here by himself.
Who was around New Orleans there?

Well, uh, Harry Shields was here. The Dixieland Band was gone. New Orleans Rhythm Kings were in Chicago. It was Paul Marys and George Brunas, and they were up there. I think there was a, most everybody was kind of out of town at that time. At least when I came over here, there wasn't very much doing.
Who was in the band with Wingy that you worked with?

Well, the only one that I remember now is Al Jordi, saxophonist, clarinet. That's the only one I remember. Uh, Steve Loicanna, I think, was playing bass. I'm sure that, uh, that's about the ones I remember now.
Oh, yeah. That was the Isle of, wait a minute, in Biloxi, the Isle of, uh, Capri was over there.
Well, I think it was the Bonifesto Hotel.
Did you ever?
Yeah, we worked out on a pier, on a dance, dance pavilion. Mm-hmm. On the pier. It isn't there anymore.
Did you use Biloxi Boys over there?
No, he got boys from here. Mm-hmm. I met Sharky, they all used to come over there on Sundays to hear us. Oh, yeah.
Do you remember a piano player around in Beaumont, mostly, I think he was, called Lazy Daddy? No. He was a colored guy?
No, no.
Yeah, I just wondered, because he, I think, worked around with different people. You worked in several places in Louisiana, haven't you, other than New Orleans?

Yeah, Sweetport. And, uh, when I was working out of Sweetport, we sort of met in headquarters up there, worked in, uh, old Alexander and, uh, and Baton Rouge, all around. Uh, I've been around Sweetport there for quite a while.
Did they have, uh, some pretty good musicians around there that your name is outstanding?
No. No. I have a, we're about the only jazz band around there.
And who was with you after that?

Oh, Terry Shand and, uh, and, uh, let's see. Terry, Terry Shand and I, we came and joined another band there, and it was called Youngberg Marin. It was about a nine or ten piece band. It was hotel work. But there was a band over at the Washington Hotel called, uh, the Louisiana Ramblers, Tim Kelly, and, uh, some, he's still in Louisiana, or Mississippi, Jackson, Mississippi, I think. And, uh, Pat and Bobby Dequeer, the boys, one played trumpet and one trombone, they were very good. But they weren't from Sweetport. They used to work up there a lot. Let's see, that's about a minute or two. What about Monk Hazel? Did you know him down here? Yeah, I met him here on some of the trips here. Mm-hmm.
Let's see. Uh, hold on. I hate to get started on anything. We'll just let it run off, huh, Paul? Yeah. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.
I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know.
I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I don't want to get started on anything. We'll just let it run off, Paul?
Mm-hmm .
Mm-hmm . Yeah . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
I'll come back and let me sit.
All right, man. Whatever you say. If you got it, do it.
